newsitem.title: USA: NYS says its welfare plan meets federal guidelines.
newsitem.headline: NYS says its welfare plan meets federal guidelines.

text.p: New York State on Tuesday staunchly defended the new welfare plan it sent to the federal government for approval, saying the outline met all the requirements despite Washington's apparent objections.

Brian Wing, acting commissioner, state Department of Social Services, also requested the federal government to correct published reports that said New York risked losing $1 million a day for every day it waited for its new, nearly $2.4 billion grant. He added guidance provided by Washington backed his position on this issue.

Like other states that have trimmed their welfare rolls, New York State stands to capture a windfall, estimated at as high as $450 million in the first year of new federal law, because the new block grant does not reflect the drop in the number of recipients.
New York was estimated to be at risk of losing $1 million a day by prorating over one year a smaller, $350 million projection of the difference between its old block grant and the new one.

The state, which has around 1.1 million people on welfare, has one of the nation's biggest and most costly programs. New York City also is widely considered vulnerable under the new rules because it has about 66 percent of the welfare caseload.

Wing blasted the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services for the way it informed New York that its plan did not pass muster, saying a newspaper article published on Tuesday and a brief telephone call that it received on Monday were the first indications it had that there was a problem.

The New York Times, in its Tuesday edition, quoted a spokesman for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services as saying, "We have a problem with the completeness of New York's plan, and we have informed the state of our concerns." The official added the department believed the problem could be solved.

The paper described the problem as New York's failure to formally adopt the time limits set in the new federal law, which says federal funds cannot be used to aid any family for more than "60 months," a period that need not be consecutive.

The state's acting commissioner, in a letter to the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Social Services, Donna Shalala, that was released to reporters, said that Gov. George Pataki fully intended to put five-year time limits in place, adding legislation had been submitted to accomplish this.

Part of the dispute appeared to center on how the new federal welfare law, which only became law in late August, was being interpreted as Wing wrote that there was no provision that the time limit be included in the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PL 104-193).
He added the guidance provided by the federal government did not mention the time limit, and stopped just short of saying New York had been unfairly singled out.
"We also understand that there are other states which have had their plans certified that do not have the legal authority in place to carry out five-year time limits," he wrote.

"Notwithstanding these facts, let me assure you that Gov. Pataki is committed to instituting time limits on the receipt of welfare payments in New York, consistent with the requrements of PL 104-193," he added.
